Radicular cervical spondylosis

A 1992 single-arm study reported a 94.4% categorical response after combined laser and Traditional Chinese Medicine, but it cannot show how much improvement came from the laser. A related cervical-herniation comparison does not directly test this diagnosis.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

A 1992 single-arm study reported a 94.4% categorical response after combined laser and Traditional Chinese Medicine, but it cannot show how much improvement came from the laser. A related cervical-herniation comparison does not directly test this diagnosis.

Summary of the Evidence

One unique publication directly addresses radicular cervical spondylosis: a 1992 single-arm report in 90 patients. A narrowly mapped cervical-disc-herniation comparison is relevant to the neck region but concerns a different diagnosis and high-intensity laser. An older mixed radicular-pain report mentioned in prior records could not be validated as a matching source and is not counted here.

Human and clinical evidence

Li reported that 94.4% of participants met the article's categorical definition of effective after laser was combined with Traditional Chinese Medicine. There was no control group, and the contribution of laser cannot be separated from the co-treatment or natural change. The related Yilmaz study compared high-intensity laser with a combination of transcutaneous nerve stimulation and ultrasound for cervical disc herniation; it is not a direct study of radicular cervical spondylosis and does not validate the older result (Li 1992 Yilmaz et al. 2020).

Animal evidence

No relevant animal study was identified.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone laboratory evidence specific to this diagnosis was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The 1992 paper reports a laser intervention with Traditional Chinese Medicine, but the available database record does not give enough verified parameters to state wavelength, dose, or session schedule. The adjacent cervical-herniation study used high-intensity laser, which is a different modality and should not be used to fill missing settings for the older study.

Interpretation

The reported response rate is descriptive and uncontrolled. It supports neither a laser-specific effect nor a reliable estimate of benefit for contemporary PBM in radicular cervical spondylosis.

Evidence strength in source summarySymptoms after combined laser and traditional medicine: Very low Laser-specific effect: Very low
Publications and records2 unique titles when the adjacent mapping is shown

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The direct evidence is one older 90-person single-arm study combining laser with Traditional Chinese Medicine, so improvement cannot be attributed to laser. A cervical disc herniation comparison is only adjacent evidence and tests high-intensity laser for a different diagnosis. A controlled study with a defined radicular population and laser-only comparison is needed.
